detail.scope: Commercial-sector electricity sales and average price by state, as reported to EIA. Data centers are billed mostly in the commercial class, so this is a proxy for their load, not a measurement of it.

sources.name: ERCOT
sources.scope: Large generators with a full interconnection study requested, from the monthly Generator Interconnection Status report for Texas. Includes projects from study through commissioning.

sources.name: NYISO
sources.scope: Projects in the New York interconnection queue as NYISO publishes them.

sources.name: MISO
sources.scope: Projects in the Midcontinent generator interconnection queue, all statuses as MISO publishes them.

sources.name: Southwest Power Pool
sources.scope: Generator interconnection requests across the south-central US, all statuses as SPP publishes them, withdrawn requests counted separately.

sources.name: CAISO
sources.scope: Active generator interconnection requests on the California ISO grid, from the public queue report. Completed and withdrawn projects are counted separately.

analysis.body:
The five grid operators represented here — ERCOT, NYISO, MISO, SPP, and CAISO — collectively show more than 1.3 million megawatts of generation and storage waiting in interconnection queues as of September 3, 2026, spread across roughly 8,365 separate requests. These are projects that have asked to connect to the grid but have not necessarily been built or approved; they range from early study phases through near-completion, and the figures are not additive across operators because each source uses its own eligibility rules and geographic scope. What they reveal is the shape of developer intent: solar dominates in Texas (150,347 MW), California (18,896 MW), and MISO (144,902 MW), while NYISO's queue is overwhelmingly classified as "other" at 291,136 MW out of its 319,095 MW total, a category that in New York's reporting absorbs offshore wind and several hybrid resource types.

For readers focused on AI data centers, the fuel categories that most directly shadow data center load growth are storage and gas, because batteries provide the fast-response backup that large campuses require and gas turbines are increasingly proposed as always-on firm capacity behind the meter or nearby. On those two fuels, ERCOT leads with 159,820 MW of storage and 78,092 MW of gas in queue — figures that dwarf every other operator shown here and reflect the intense data center development pressure on the Texas grid. SPP follows with 52,913 MW of storage and 47,392 MW of gas, and MISO shows 68,429 MW of storage and 30,236 MW of gas; CAISO's active queue carries 46,944 MW of storage against only 916 MW of gas, consistent with California's policy constraints on new fossil capacity.

The commercial electricity sales figures, reported separately by EIA for June 2026, show Texas leading all listed states at 15,754 gigawatt-hours of commercial-sector sales, with Virginia at 7,771 GWh and California at 10,025 GWh; these are proxies for, not measurements of, data center consumption, since data centers are billed under commercial tariffs alongside offices, retail, and other users. Virginia's figure is particularly notable because northern Virginia hosts the world's densest concentration of data centers yet its 7,771 GWh trails California despite a far lower average commercial price of 10.99 cents per kilowatt-hour against California's 27.33 cents. The queue and sales data together will next clarify how much of ERCOT's enormous storage backlog actually advances through studies to signed interconnection agreements, since that progression — not the queue total itself — is the real indicator of whether firm capacity is being built fast enough to serve the load.
